a recognizable common interpretation. Your task is comparative: after reading
the book's sources and full argument, determine which specific interpretation

BOOK ENTRY
The gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Heb 4:2) · see Gospel, ch. 5

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 52:7 — How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
Isaiah 2:3 — And many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
Jeremiah 31:33 — But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Hebrews 4:2 — For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/05-gospel.adoc

Ask an AI for the gospel in a sentence, and it will hand you the average of what most of Christianity teaches:

The Gospel is the good news that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day, so that through repentance and faith in Him alone we can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and given eternal life.

People will tell you this is the core message, summarized by Paul in 1 Corinthians 15 and proclaimed throughout the New Testament.

Moreover, brethren, I declare to you the gospel which I preached to you… by which also you are saved, if you hold fast that word which I preached to you — unless you believed in vain.
For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures.

   
Stop here and you might think the gospel is the death and resurrection themselves; but Paul anchors it twice in the Scriptures — and his Scriptures were the Old Testament.

The word “gospel” falls in ninety-eight verses of the King James, and its verb — “preach the gospel,” “bring good tidings” — in dozens more; behind them stand one Greek word-family (euangelion, the good news; euangelizō, to announce it) and one Hebrew family (basar, to bear tidings; besorah, the tidings themselves).

Here are the titles the gospel wears, counted across the King James:

.The titles the gospel wears — and no title of death, cross, or forgiveness among them

|===
| Title | Uses
| the gospel of Christ | 11
| the gospel of God | 7
| the gospel of the kingdom | 4
| the gospel of peace | 2
| the gospel of the grace of God | 1
| the gospel of your salvation | 1
| the everlasting gospel | 1
|===

The Hebrew Revelation gives that last title a body: where the Greek reads “everlasting gospel,” the Hebrew text hands the messenger a certain stone tablet (gilyon) “to make known to those dwelling upon the earth” (Revelation 14:6) — the good news, written in stone.

Of these, John the Baptist, Jesus, and His disciples preached the gospel of the kingdom — and preached it before the cross.

And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.

Mark records the herald-cry in full:

Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God, And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.

Hear what the gospel asks for.
Not “accept this fact,” but “repent ye, and believe” — turn, trust, and obey; for to believe, as the Love, Knowing, Faith, and Belief chapter will prove, is to obey.

The word for preaching it is the herald’s word — kēryssō, what a royal crier does: he announces the decree of the one who sent him, and the fitting response is allegiance.

Isaiah gives the publication its single sentence:

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

There is the whole of it compressed to three words: “Thy God reigneth.”
The Hebrew verb here is basar; the Greek Old Testament renders it with euangelizō, the origin of the English evangelize; and Paul quotes this very verse as gospel-preaching: “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace” (Romans 10:15).

Look once more at the herald’s third clause: “that publisheth salvation” — the Hebrew is yeshuah: the Old Testament’s gospel-verse publishes Jesus by name.

Mark where the herald stands — upon the mountains; what a mountain is, the Mountain chapter will prove.

Nahum carries Isaiah's verse almost word for word — and adds the hearer's marching orders:

Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off.

If we are to hearken to the herald's cry, the stakes of understanding the symbolic language of the Sun, Moon, and Stars run much higher.

When Jesus stood up in His hometown synagogue to announce His own commission, listen to which scripture He chose:

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,

The passage is Isaiah 61:1-2, and its closing proclamation — “the acceptable year of the LORD” — is the year of release, the seventh year of Deuteronomy 15, when debts are cancelled and captives go free. [Footnote: The full derivation is in the Liberty chapter.]
The gospel, in Jesus’ own chosen words, is a royal proclamation of release — and He sat down and told them, “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears” (Luke 4:21).
(That year of release is dated to the Day of Atonement, AD 29, in Time Tested Tradition; what matters here is which text Jesus reached for when He defined His gospel.)

Now the hinge that the common definition cannot survive.
Jesus preached this gospel — the whole of it — before He died:

From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

From the opening of His ministry, years before the cross, He was already preaching the gospel of the kingdom (Matthew 4:23), and commanding hearers to “believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15).
If the gospel were the message about His death and resurrection, He could not have preached it for three years while both were still ahead of Him — nor commanded men to believe it before it existed.
Even when He told the twelve plainly what was ahead, “they understood none of these things” (Luke 18:34).

What He preached was the arrival of God’s reign and the way of life under it: the kingdom and its terms.
The gospel is the message Jesus taught, not merely the message about Jesus.

Nor was it new even to Him.
The book of Hebrews drops a line most readers pass over: the gospel was preached long before, to the generation in the wilderness —

For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.

“Unto them” is Israel at Sinai.
The same gospel-word describes what was proclaimed there — and what was proclaimed there was a kingdom:

And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.

God, having broken the siege of Egypt and set the captives at liberty, declares His reign over them and calls them to enter it as His kingdom.
That is the gospel of the kingdom — preached at Sinai.
Earlier still, to Abraham:

And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed.

“Preached before the gospel” is a single Greek word, proeuangelizomai — pre-gospeled.
Abraham received the gospel, and its reach — all nations — is the same reach it has from first to last.
One gospel runs the length of Scripture: Abraham, Sinai, Jesus, the apostles.
Revelation even gives it its proper adjective, and states its content one final time:

And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people, Saying with a loud voice, Fear God, and give glory to him; for the hour of his judgment is come: and worship him that made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and the fountains of waters.

Everlasting — a thing cannot be everlasting and also have begun at the cross.
And read what the everlasting gospel says when it opens its mouth: fear God, give Him glory, worship the Maker, the judgment is come.
The last gospel-preaching in the Bible is the herald’s cry of the reigning Creator — the same three words Isaiah gave it.

If the gospel announces a King’s reign, it necessarily carries terms, for a king reigns by covenant.
Here the threads draw together: the gospel of the kingdom is the covenant of the kingdom.
And the covenant, Scripture is careful to say, was never scrapped and replaced — it was renewed.
The promise everyone calls the “new covenant” rests on a Hebrew word, chadash, whose root means renew, repair, rebuild:

Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.

And it came to pass after this, that Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD.

David does not ask for a spirit he never had; Joash does not build a different temple.
Chadash restores what already stands.
So the “new” covenant is the same covenant, renewed — and Jeremiah, who gave the promise, says precisely what changes and what does not:

Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel… Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers… which my covenant they brake… I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.

The fault lay not with the covenant but with the people — “my covenant they brake.”
The law is the same law; the terms are the same terms.
What changes is the location — from tablets of stone to the inward parts, from a code outside us to a writing within.
Same covenant, new surface.
This is why Jesus could insist, in the very sermon where He pressed the law to its depths:

Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.

Not destroy — fulfil.
And “fulfil” is the Greek plēroō: to fill full, to fill to the brim — the exact opposite of “destroy” (kataluō, to tear down).
Jesus did not come to abolish the law, nor to complete it and retire it, but to fill it full — to preach it in its fullness, packing back the weight the surface reading had drained away.

Filling full is precisely what He does next: “Ye have heard that it was said… but I say unto you,” pressing past the act to the heart behind it (Matthew 5:21-22) — filling each commandment full, writing it where Jeremiah said it would be written.
The Sermon on the Mount is the renewed covenant in motion: the same Torah, filled full and taught from the inside.
This is the message Jesus taught — not a new religion about Himself, but the ancient covenant of the kingdom, renewed and written on the heart.

The gospel, then, is no abolition of the law of Moses but its establishment — “we establish the law,” as Paul says (Romans 3:31).
The gospel of the kingdom is the law of that kingdom: the Torah preached in the wilderness, the constitution of God’s reign, the very law the prophets foresaw going forth from Zion when the King at last reigns from His mountain:

…Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.

One law, from first to last: preached in the wilderness, written now upon the heart, and one day issuing from Zion over all the earth (Micah 4:2 says the same).

This is why Scripture speaks of the gospel in a way that makes no sense for a mere announcement of facts: it speaks of obeying it.
“They have not all obeyed the gospel” (Romans 10:16); the Lord returns “in flaming fire taking vengeance on them… that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thessalonians 1:8); and Peter asks, “what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?”
(1 Peter 4:17).
Information is believed or doubted; nobody obeys a news bulletin.
But a king’s proclamation with terms is obeyed or defied — and Scripture says the gospel is the kind of thing men will be judged for not obeying.

Mark how Paul glosses his own words inside that first verse:

But they have not all obeyed the gospel.
For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report?

Obeyed in one sentence, believed in the next — one act under two names.
That is what believe means in Scripture’s mouth: not thinking a thing true, but trusting enough to obey.
The equation runs both directions — the Greek under “believeth not” in John 3:36 locks it from the other side. [Footnote: The word is opened in the Love, Knowing, Faith, and Belief chapter.]
To believe the gospel is to obey the King.

Where, then, is the cross in all this?
Exactly where Scripture sets it — as the act that secures the kingdom, not as the whole content of the announcement:

When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.

“It is finished” completes the work that ratifies the covenant in blood.
The cross is indispensable — it is how the kingdom is purchased and the renewed covenant sealed.
But the purchase is not the proclamation.
The proof stands where we left it: Jesus preached the whole gospel of the kingdom for years before Calvary.

Here the fair objection rises: does not Paul himself define the gospel as the death and resurrection?
He does say it plainly:

For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.

Read closely, this confirms rather than overturns what we have seen.
Twice Paul anchors it “according to the scriptures” — the death and resurrection fulfill what the prophets had already announced; they are how the long-promised kingdom is secured, not a new message that cancels it.
And he is expressly defending the resurrection here — the burden of the whole of 1 Corinthians 15 — summarizing the hinge of the gospel, not redrawing its borders.
Where Paul opens a letter by stating his gospel at length, the kingdom is unmistakable:

Paul… separated unto the gospel of God, (Which he had promised afore by his prophets in the holy scriptures,) Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh; And declared to be the Son of God with power… by the resurrection from the dead.

Every clause is kingdom language.
The gospel was “promised afore by his prophets” — the same ancient announcement, not a novelty.
Its subject is the “seed of David” — the rightful heir to the throne.
And the resurrection “declared” Him “the Son of God with power” — the enthronement of the King.

Paul’s gospel is that the Son of David has been raised and installed as Lord; the cross and the empty tomb are how He took the throne.
That is the gospel of the kingdom, told from the side of the King’s accession.

It is why Paul can stake everything on there being only one gospel — “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you… let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8) — the very gospel, he reminds the same readers, that was “preached before… unto Abraham” (Galatians 3:8).
And it is why, at the end of the age, the message has not changed:

And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come.

The last gospel preached before the end still wears the only content-title it has ever worn.

Now return to the sentence the AI gave us, and grade it.
Every clause in it is true, and every clause can be found in Scripture — the death for sins, the burial, the third day, the call to repentance and faith.
But as a definition it fails the full witness of Scripture.

The word we thought we owned opens up like all the rest.
The mountain is the kingdom; the gospel is the herald’s cry that the kingdom has come — “Thy God reigneth” — published upon the mountains and carried to every nation: the siege broken, the captives freed, the covenant renewed onto hearts, the King enthroned.
Read it as a private transaction and it shrinks to a fraction of itself.
Read it as Scripture defines it, and the turning of the nations that closed the last chapter stands revealed for what it is: not the spread of information about a man, but the kingdom of God going forth to fill the earth.

After the resurrection the risen King sent His heralds to the nations, and the commission names the gospel's content one last time: “teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt 28:19-20).
The commission's verb is matheteusate — disciple the nations — and Isaiah had already defined the word: “bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples” (Isa 8:16); to disciple the nations is to seal the law among them.
What had He commanded them?
Where our Bibles read “all therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do” — a sentence at war with the chapter of woes that follows it — the Hebrew Matthew reads:

On the seat of Moses sit the Pharisees and the sages.
Now, all that he says to you, keep and do; but according to their ordinances and their deeds, do not do — for they say, and do not.

All that he says — Moses: the seat carries the authority of the one it belongs to, not of the men who sit in it.
Their “ordinances” are taqqanot — the technical term for rabbinic enactments, the man-made rules of the oral torah, the very “tradition of the elders” (Matt 15:2) that “made the commandment of God of none effect” (Matt 15:6): keep Moses; drop the enactments.
And the Hebrew commission closes on a word the Greek lost — have them keep “all the words which I have commanded you — forever”: the King enthroned, sending heralds to every nation with the law of the kingdom, taught, kept, forever.
